newsitem.title: MEXICO: Tribasa to restructure highway finances.
newsitem.headline: Tribasa to restructure highway finances.

text.p: Grupo Tribasa is negotiating with the government and a group of banks to restructure finances for eight highway projects, a top company executive told Reuters.

"I could not say how much but we are talking about eight projects that would qualify to begin with...I can only say that we are talking about substantial amounts," said Manuel Delgado, vice-president of finance at Tribasa in an interview last last week.
The Mexican government estimates it will channel 14 billion pesos, or 0.6 percent of GDP, into easing the financial burden of highway projects for private companies granted concessions to build them.
Delgado said the financial restructuring also involved construction companies Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo and ICA.
All those firms made over-optimistic projections of revenues when building the toll roads, and were additionally hit by the December 1994 peso devaluation.

"Banks, construction companies and the government are involved. We are talking about highway projects with bank debts and a general scheme in which negotiations will take place for each highway," he added.

Tribasa operates six highway concessions, with different degrees of participation, notably Mexico City-Guadalajara, Cuernavaca-Acapulco and Mazatlan-Culiacan. Tribasa also operates all highway concessions granted in the Mexico City area.
"Most of our highways, which are in the Mexico City area, are securitized. That is, we handed over our rights to a trust and will receive funds in due course," Delgado said.

A Tribasa executive report says that securitization has totalled $645 million. Securitization backed by a CPO issue allowed $227 million to flow into Tribasa's coffers, after paying off debt and commissions.
"We are no longer responsible for those projects, as we are just operators. Our revenues are not affected, whether they work or not," he said.
"When the securitization process ends, we will have to see how to proceed so as to restructure (the finances), but we will see about that when the time comes," he added.
"What I can say is that none of the highways has the traffic flow that was forecast," Delgado said.
Delgado also said that expectations of growth in the construction industry would allow sustained increases in Tribasa's margins beginning in the fourth quarter of 1996.
